To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exogenous amylases can be effective in improving starch digestion and milk production in lactating cows.
an exogenous amyla- se supplement increased ruminal starch digestion and decreased ruminal acetate concentration and tended to increase propionate concentration.

the amylase supplement increased the true digestibility of organic mater in the rumen and the concentration of propionate in the rumen, without affecting the total-tract digestion of organic matter and starch.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of an amylase supplement on nutrient digestion in dairy cattle fed diets with different starch levels.
the effects of a novel enzyme additive on the ruminal digestion of starch, the microbial community and ruminal fermentation in dairy cattle.
the effect of an amylase supplement on the digestion and metabolism of starch in the rumen and total tract of dairy cows fed low- or high-starch diets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the exogenous enzyme supplement increased starch digestibility in the rumen of first-lactation dairy cows, but this did not affect nutrient digestibility at the total- tract level.
the exogenous enzyme increased the digestibility of organic and starch matter in the rumen, and the increased starch digestion was compensated at the total- tract level.
exogenous amylases are effective to enhance starch digestion in the ruminant, and that the response depends on the dietary context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

exogenous amylases are a promising tool to increase starch utilization by the rumen microbial community, and this may be particularly important for diets with high starch content and low fiber content.
exogenous amylases may be a useful tool for increasing starch digestion in dairy cows fed high-starch diets.

the addition of amylase to high- or low-starch diets improved ruminal starch digestion in first-lacting cows without negative effects on ruminal digestion of fiber, microbial protein supply, intake, or milk production.
The main takeaway from our work is that
amylase supplementation can improve starch digestion in dairy cattle fed low-starch diets, and that this can occur without negative effects on ruminal fermentation and fiber digestion.
exogenous enzymes may be a useful tool to improve starch utilization in the dairy cow.
amylase supplementation may improve ruminal starch digestion in dairy cows, but this effect is compensated by increased starch digestion in the small intestine.
